scenes.visual: Title: Temperature, Water and Biomes. Show wet forest and desert beside temperature and rainfall symbols.

scenes.tts: Temperature and water, and how they vary through the year, largely decide which biome a place supports. A biome is a large region with similar climate and dominant vegetation and animals. Tropical wet forest fits warmth and rain in every month. Desert fits scarce rain. So climate gives us a first prediction of the vegetation. We can compare that prediction with what actually grows there. But climate does not fix the biome. Fire and soils modify the pattern.

scenes.visual: Lead with warm, year-round rain beside tropical wet forest, then scarce rain beside desert. Show monthly temperature and rainfall strips, not just annual averages. Link climate to a vegetation prediction, then to observed vegetation; introduce fire and soil icons as modifiers.

scenes.tts: Under the same rain, soils differ in water holding capacity and nutrients. That can support different vegetation. Staver and colleagues analysed tropical tree cover in Africa, Australia and South America. Across a wide rainfall range with a short dry season, places were mostly savanna or forest. Fire was associated with keeping areas open. A changing climate also need not mean an immediate change of biome. That depends on dispersal, soils, fire and time.

scenes.visual: Show the same rainfall over soils with different water storage and nutrients. Show observed forest and savanna tree cover, with fire associated with open vegetation. Do not label these as proven stable states or depict an experiment. End with climate changing before vegetation, with dispersal, soils, fire and time as conditions.

scenes.tts: Where does that climate come from? Sunlight striking Earth at a slant spreads over more ground. Over the year, the tropics receive more energy and the poles less. The atmosphere and oceans carry heat poleward. Near the equator, warm moist air rises, cools and drops rain. Dry air flows poleward aloft and sinks in the subtropics. It warms as it sinks, suppressing rain. This is the idealized Hadley cell. It helps explain wet equatorial regions and subtropical deserts. Mountains add wet windward slopes and dry rain shadows.

scenes.visual: Show equal sunlight beams spreading over different ground areas, then a tropical-to-polar energy gradient with atmospheric and oceanic heat transport. Animate the idealized Hadley cell: rising, cooling, raining air at the equator and sinking, warming air over subtropical desert. Finish with a windward-rain/leeward-rain-shadow cross section. Omit solar arithmetic.

scenes.tts: Annual rainfall totals hide timing. Knapp and colleagues used shelters in a native grassland and reapplied rain. They kept the total constant but made events fewer and larger. Soil moisture became more variable, plant production fell, and species diversity rose. That result applies to that grassland. Repeat it elsewhere before generalizing. Compare unsheltered plots with sheltered plots receiving the natural pattern, too. That checks whether the shelters themselves change the result.

scenes.visual: Show replicated, randomly assigned grassland plots. Compare sheltered natural-pattern irrigation with fewer, larger events at the same total. Include unsheltered natural-rain controls to check shelter effects. Show the observed increase in soil-moisture variability, decrease in production and increase in diversity, explicitly bounded to the studied grassland.

scenes.tts: Organisms also experience local microclimates. Beneath forest canopies, understories were cooler on average and in their hottest temperatures than nearby open habitat. In cold conditions, canopies warmed the understory. The temperature an organism experiences is not the station's. Climate predicts biomes roughly. Local conditions modify that prediction.

scenes.visual: Show paired temperature loggers beneath canopy and in nearby open habitat. Depict lower mean and maximum understory temperatures, but warming under canopy in cold conditions, without numerical offsets. Return to the climate-to-vegetation prediction with local conditions added.

scenes.tts: A smaller point: a climate diagram helps read the seasonal pattern. The lesson's made up station stays warm and humid all year. Its tropical rainforest climate fits tropical wet forest. That is a hypothesis to test against the vegetation actually present.

scenes.visual: Label this closing scene 'A smaller point: reading climate'. Use the lesson's made-up station chart, with rainfall above the linked temperature line in every month; show the Af climate label beside a tropical wet forest prediction and a prompt to check observed vegetation. No classification arithmetic.
End card: Temperature, water and seasonality organize biomes. Fire, soils, rainfall timing and microclimate modify the pattern.
